key_facts: **DRESS** is a severe, delayed drug reaction: rash, fever, **facial oedema**, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement.
Latency **2–8 weeks**; culprits: allopurinol, carbamazepine and other aromatic anticonvulsants, lamotrigine, sulfonamides/dapsone, minocycline, vancomycin.
The liver is the commonest organ involved; also kidney, lung, heart, thyroid. Mortality about 2–10%.
Stop the drug and arrange **same-day hospital assessment**; systemic steroids tapered slowly over 6–12 weeks.
Follow up thyroid function and glucose for 1–2 years (late autoimmunity).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **DRESS** (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; also called DIHS) is a delayed, multi-organ reaction with fever, rash and internal organ involvement. Mortality is about **2–10%**.

sub: About 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 exposures to high-risk drugs; adults more than children.
HLA risk alleles: HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol), HLA-A*31:01 (carbamazepine in Europeans).

ul: Type IVb (Th2 / eosinophil) reaction with **sequential herpesvirus reactivation** (HHV-6, then EBV/CMV), which explains the relapsing course.
Culprits: **allopurinol**, **carbamazepine**, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, **sulfonamides/dapsone**, minocycline, vancomycin, abacavir/nevirapine, strontium.
Latency **2–8 weeks** (the longest of the severe drug reactions).
**"It's just a drug rash"**: facial swelling, fever and abnormal blood tests mean a systemic emergency.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: DRESS combines a **drug-specific T-cell attack** with **herpesvirus reactivation**.

mech.t: The drug or a metabolite binds HLA molecules and activates T cells (often in genetically susceptible people).
IL-5 and other Th2 cytokines drive eosinophilia and tissue infiltration.
HHV-6, then EBV and CMV reactivate, sustaining inflammation and relapses.
Infiltrating T cells and eosinophils injure the liver, kidney, lung and heart.
Immune dysregulation after recovery can cause thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes.

histo: Interface or spongiotic dermatitis with dense perivascular lymphocytes and eosinophils; not specific. RegiSCAR scoring combines clinical and lab features.

ul: Morbilliform rash that becomes infiltrated and oedematous, often **over 50% of body surface**; may become exfoliative.
**Facial oedema** (key sign); fever above 38 °C; **lymphadenopathy**.
Blood: eosinophilia (over 1.5 × 10⁹/L), atypical lymphocytes.
**Organ involvement**: liver (commonest), kidney, lung, heart (myocarditis), thyroid.
Course over weeks to months with relapses; **late autoimmune disease** (thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes).
**RegiSCAR** score grades the likelihood of DRESS.

fig.caption: Widespread morbilliform eruption of DRESS — check for fever, facial oedema, nodes, eosinophils and liver function.

sub: Highest risk with recent start, high dose, renal impairment and HLA-B*58:01 (common in Han Chinese, Thai and Korean people).

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: FBC with differential and film, LFT, U&E, urinalysis, troponin/ECG if symptomatic, TFT, lipase, HHV-6 PCR and skin biopsy. Patch testing later can help identify the culprit.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Viral exanthem, lymphoma (especially angioimmunoblastic), hypereosinophilic syndrome, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki disease, simple [morbilliform drug eruption](condition:morbilliform-drug-eruption).

sections.title: Management

ul: **Stop the culprit**, document, Yellow Card, and avoid for life (including cross-reacting drugs).
**Same-day hospital assessment** if fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia or abnormal LFTs.
Mild disease without significant organ involvement: potent topical steroids.
With organ involvement: **systemic corticosteroids** (e.g. prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) **tapered slowly over 6–12 weeks**: rapid tapers cause relapse.
Monitor organs for months, and check **TFT and glucose** for 1–2 years.

blocks: Recognise, stop, refer, document, Yellow Card. After discharge: support the specialist steroid taper (steroid card if prolonged) and monitor TFT/glucose per the specialist letter.

ladder.t: Stop the culprit; record the allergy; Yellow Card.
Potent topical steroid under specialist care; monitor bloods.

refer.t: Rash + fever + facial oedema / lymph nodes 2–8 weeks after a new high-risk drug.
Follow-up TFT and glucose for 1–2 years (late autoimmunity).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Fever + rash + facial oedema or lymphadenopathy **2–8 weeks** after a new anticonvulsant, allopurinol or sulfonamide: **same-day admission** (hepatitis, nephritis and myocarditis can follow).
Allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01), carbamazepine (HLA-B*15:02) and lamotrigine are high-risk starts: counsel to report a rash early.
Fulminant hepatitis, interstitial nephritis, pneumonitis, myocarditis; death.
Autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, alopecia areata after recovery.
Recovery over weeks to months; relapses during steroid taper are common.

pearls: DRESS has the **longest latency** of the severe drug reactions (2–8 weeks).
"**Allopurinol + CKD + recent start + rash** = DRESS/SJS risk": dose adjustment and HLA-B*58:01 awareness.

quiz.q: What is the typical latency of DRESS?

quiz.a: Allopurinol, carbamazepine (and other aromatic anticonvulsants), sulfonamides/dapsone, minocycline.

quiz.q: Which organ is most often involved?

quiz.a: Rapid tapers cause relapse (linked to herpesvirus reactivation).
